title: Homeowner Identification During Registration
description: Homeowner provides personally identifiable information (name, address, device identifiers) during account registration and camera/sensor enrollment, creating identification risk at the source.

title: Data Interception During Enrollment
description: Camera/sensor enrollment data and credentials transmitted between Homeowner and Home Hub could be intercepted by unauthorized parties during transit.

title: Unauthorized Data Disclosure at Home Hub
description: Home Hub may store or process enrolled camera/sensor data in ways that could lead to unauthorized disclosure to third parties or beyond intended scope.

title: Linkability of Enrolled Devices to Homeowner
description: Home Hub may link camera/sensor data to homeowner identity, enabling correlation of device usage patterns with personal information.

title: Access code in transit could be intercepted and linked to guest identity
description: The temporary access code transmitted from Guest User to Home Hub could be intercepted by an attacker, potentially allowing them to link the code to the guest's identity or infer guest presence at the property.

title: Access code metadata could identify guest presence
description: Metadata about the access code transmission (timing, frequency, or pattern) could be used to identify that a guest is present at or attempting to access the property, even without the code itself.

title: Home Hub could allow code sharing or unauthorized access
description: The Home Hub process could store or log the access code in a way that allows it to be shared with others, or could be compromised to allow unauthorized access using the code.

title: Guest may inadvertently share access code with others
description: The guest user may share the temporary access code with others (family members, visitors, etc.) who then gain unauthorized access to the property.

title: Sensor events can be linked to individuals
description: Motion, door, and sensor events collected by the Home Hub can be linked to specific individuals or activities within the home, enabling correlation of events to particular persons.

title: Sensor events may identify individuals
description: The collected events (motion, door, sensor) can be used to identify individuals present in the home, potentially revealing their presence, movements, and activities.

title: Local event log may be accessible to unauthorized parties
description: The Local Event Log (DS1) stores sensitive sensor data that could be accessed by unauthorized individuals if proper access controls and encryption are not in place.

title: Excessive sensor data collection
description: The Home Hub may collect more sensor data than necessary for its intended purpose, potentially including data that is not required for the specific functionality.

title: Data Interception During Upload
description: Video clips transmitted from Home Hub to Cloud Video Storage could be intercepted by unauthorized parties during transit, potentially exposing sensitive surveillance footage.

title: Metadata Linkability in Transit
description: Metadata about the data flow (e.g., timestamps, source/destination identifiers) could be used to link video clips to specific individuals or locations.

title: Unauthorized Access to Stored Video
description: Cloud Video Storage may be accessed by unauthorized parties, leading to disclosure of recorded surveillance footage.

title: Identification from Stored Video
description: Stored video clips may contain personally identifiable information that could be used to identify individuals.

title: Data Integrity Compromise in Transit
description: Video data could be modified or corrupted during transmission from Home Hub to Cloud Video Storage.

title: Explicit data disclosure to third-party backend
description: Home Hub (P1) forwards real-time motion alert data to Mobile App Backend (P2), constituting an explicit disclosure of personal data across a system boundary. The motion data may contain information about occupants' presence, movement patterns, and potentially their location.
assumptions: Motion data is considered personal data as it can reveal presence and activity patterns of individuals in the home.

title: Linkability via meta-data in transit
description: Data in transit between Home Hub and Mobile App Backend may contain meta-data (timestamps, device identifiers, connection info) that could be used to link the motion alert to specific individuals or locations, potentially enabling tracking or profiling.
assumptions: Meta-data accompanying the motion alert transmission could be exploited to identify or link data to individuals.
uncertainty_note: Assuming meta-data is transmitted alongside the alert

title: Identification through motion data transmission
description: The motion alert data itself, when transmitted, could be used to identify individuals or infer their presence at a specific location and time, potentially revealing sensitive information about occupants' routines and habits.
assumptions: Motion data patterns can be analyzed to identify individuals or infer their presence.
uncertainty_note: Depends on the granularity and context of the motion data

title: Further disclosure by destination system
description: Mobile App Backend (P2) receives the motion alert and may further process, store, or share this data with additional parties (e.g., cloud services, analytics platforms, third-party integrations), potentially amplifying the exposure of personal data beyond the intended scope.
assumptions: The backend system may have additional data sharing capabilities or integrations not visible in this DFD.
uncertainty_note: Assuming backend may have additional data sharing capabilities

title: Identification via notification metadata
description: Metadata about the motion-detected notification (e.g., timestamp, device ID, notification type) could be used to identify the homeowner's presence and activity patterns at a specific location.

title: Linkability of notification to other data
description: The notification data could be linked with other data sources (e.g., other app activities, location history) to build a profile of the homeowner's behavior and movements.

title: Data interception during transmission
description: The notification data in transit could be intercepted by unauthorized parties, potentially exposing the homeowner's location and activity information.

title: Usurpation of notification authenticity
description: The homeowner could potentially receive spoofed notifications that appear to come from the legitimate mobile app backend, leading to confusion or unauthorized actions.

title: Insufficient aggregation of device-usage analytics
description: Mobile app backend shares aggregated device-usage analytics with cloud analytics vendor. If aggregation is insufficient, individual users could potentially be re-identified through linkage with other data sources.
assumptions: Aggregation level may not be sufficient to prevent re-identification when combined with external data

title: Metadata exposure during data transmission
description: Data in transit between mobile app backend and cloud analytics vendor may contain metadata (e.g., timestamps, data volumes, request patterns) that could be used to infer information about users or the nature of the analytics being shared.
assumptions: Data transmission may not be fully anonymized or encrypted

title: Unauthorized secondary use of analytics data
description: Cloud analytics vendor may use the received device-usage analytics beyond the scope of the original agreement, potentially for purposes not consented to by the mobile app backend or its users.
assumptions: Vendor may have incentives to repurpose data for additional revenue or competitive advantage

title: Inadequate access controls at vendor
description: Cloud analytics vendor may not have sufficient access controls to prevent unauthorized access to the received analytics data by their own personnel or third parties.
assumptions: Vendor's security practices may not match the sensitivity level of the data

title: Potential regulatory non-compliance in data sharing
description: Sharing device-usage analytics with external vendor may violate privacy regulations (e.g., GDPR, CCPA) if proper consent mechanisms, data minimization, or purpose limitation requirements are not met.
assumptions: Data sharing practices may not fully comply with applicable privacy laws
